design.components: 1) core/metrics.py: Counter/Histogram registry; log-scale buckets 5 ms..120 s (~20 buckets) chosen dense around the 1-1.5 s targets; observe(name, ms, **labels) with a fixed label allowlist per metric (no ids, no text); a 10-slot per-minute ring per series for in-process windowed summaries; drain_deltas() for the flush (ring untouched); quantile(buckets, q). 2) core/metrics_flush.py: lifespan task every 60 s adding this worker's deltas into metric_minute when the SqlStore is live; 7-day retention; on DB error keep deltas and retry (bounded 60 min). 3) core/middleware.py: RequestContextMiddleware rewritten as pure ASGI middleware wrapping send(), recording time to http.response.start and to the final body chunk (more_body False) per route template; x-request-id accepted only if ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{8,64}$, else uuid4, bound via structlog contextvars. 4) agents/ideation.py turn_stream: TurnClock perf_counter marks ack, first_sentence, done and per tool call, labelled by lane (offline/model/provider), observed and written as one turn.timing log line; lives in the T28 typed event writer. 5) agents/jobs.py: job.done with seconds; job.duration histogram by kind; Board.wait counts job.wait{kind, outcome=in_time|late|failed}. 6) routers/voice.py: TTS seconds per /speak call. 7) routers/status.py: GET /api/v1/status guarded by an operator token from settings, else localhost only; aggregates only: breakers (state, open_until), store name and DB reachability, redis.is_live (T08), research pauses, budgets used, provider chain, egress block (T25), 10-minute p50/p95 per metric, job in-time ratio, alerts[] evaluated on read (first_sentence p50 > 1.5 s over 10 min, breaker open, store unreachable, research paused), and a 'scope' field saying cluster (DB) or this worker. routers/health.py adds /health/ready. POST /api/v1/status/client-timing: bounded, no ids, rate-limited first-audio beacon. 8) Log policy in core/logging.py: grounding.dropped logs problem codes and sha256(sentence)[:10]; a structlog processor replaces values of deny keys (sentence, text, reply, idea, utterance, transcript) with length+hash and truncates any other string over 200 chars.
design.data_model: metric_minute(minute timestamptz, name text, labels jsonb canonical sorted, count bigint, sum_ms double precision, buckets int[], PRIMARY KEY (minute, name, labels)); counters use count only. Metrics: turn.ack_ms, turn.first_sentence_ms, turn.done_ms{lane}, turn.tool_ms{tool}, http.response_ms{route}, job.duration_ms{kind}, job.wait{kind,outcome}, voice.tts_ms, voice.first_audio_ms, grounding.dropped{code}, breaker.open{name}.
design.algorithm: Quantile: sum bucket arrays over the window, walk cumulative counts to q x total, interpolate linearly inside the bucket. In-process ring rotates on observe by minute. Flush: swap delta dicts (single event loop, atomic), upsert with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and add arrays in Python. Status reads metric_minute for the last 10 minutes when the DB is live, else the in-process ring.
design.rollout: 1) Log policy and request-id validation now (no dependency). 2) Registry with in-process ring and the guarded status page. 3) ASGI middleware, TurnClock (with T28 task 1), job outcomes, TTS timing. 4) metric_minute migration and flush. final.tests: Quantile over known bucket arrays within one bucket; ring drops data older than 10 minutes (injected clock); flush merges two workers' deltas into one row; registry rejects unknown labels. ASGI middleware: a streaming endpoint sleeping 200 ms between chunks records >= 200 ms; a request id with a newline or 200 chars is replaced. Offline turn gives ack <= first_sentence <= done. final.risks: Label cardinality held by allowlists. A dying worker loses up to a minute of deltas (acceptable). Bucket edges bound accuracy. The redaction processor is a safety net, not the primary control. The client beacon must not become a tracking channel: no ids, bounded values, rate-limited.

verdicts.reasoning: Both read the code correctly (slots.py _required_for: idea REQUIRED 9 minus 3 plus 4 = 10 against Q_MAX = 7; idea-worded questions; research on the self-description; CONFIRMING -> GENERATING) and chose the same approach: one machine, trimmed required set, per-mode wording, cited skill/asset tags on cards, a deterministic ranker and a choice step. A also verified that AgentStartIn has no mode (routers/ideation.py:248), so the mode is unreachable today and must be exposed last. They differ on two points that matter. (1) Where the choice lives: A puts it in T27's agent-level PendingAction Choose(card) with T27's ordinal/keyword matcher; B adds SessionState.CHOOSING plus a Choice field in the elicitation session and a separate POST .../choice route. Both T27 designs already define Choose{card|lever} in the agent session, so B's CHOOSING would be a second, parallel pending-choice mechanism that T27's decide() would have to reconcile; A's fits the dependency graph. (2) Data honesty: B makes capital_band and funding_route purpose-tagged (financial consent, T19) instead of required, so the required set is 4 and never conflicts with consent; A lists capital_band as required yet says it is skipped without consent, which is self-contradictory. B also drops UNKNOWN terms (district not rated, capital not asked) and renormalises instead of A's invented defaults (capital 0.5 when unknown, district 0 when absent), never shows a card with zero skill overlap, and correctly notes that card needs/offers are business capabilities, not personal skills, so A's half-weight capability fallback for untagged cards is unsound. Final = A's structure (T27 Choose, skills.json vocabulary with en/ta/hi aliases, ship-the-mode-last rollout, ranker reasons) with B's 4-slot required set, purpose tags, UNKNOWN-dropping scoring, zero-overlap exclusion and source-count tie-break.

final.chosen: First-class experience flow on the same machine: a 4-slot experience required set with money behind financial consent, per-mode question text and order, research gated on a real idea, cards enriched with cited skills/assets tags, a deterministic ranker that drops unknown terms, and T27's Choose(card) pending action for picking an opportunity
final.why_chosen: It fixes the modelling error (a flow, not a reworded required set) inside the existing selector, engine and the T27 conversation state, so there is one pending-choice mechanism for cards and levers. The required set fits Q_MAX by construction, money questions honour consent, and the ranker is code-decided (0002), explainable and cited, offline, with no invented values when a fact is unknown.

verdicts.reasoning: Both found the same cause (s.private read only by research; providers.chain()/judge() never see the session; /voice/speak takes free text with no session; browser SpeechRecognition sends audio to Google in Chrome; the planned notice keys on the answering provider) and the same fix: a per-session egress policy computed before the first turn from configuration, privacy and consent, chain(policy)/judge(policy), session-scoped /speak, a versioned may-reach notice, and browser STT named and gated. The deciding difference is fit with neighbouring themes: both teams' T15 designs build a single outbound gate (A3: core/outbound.py, B5: core/egress.py) for every external call. B enforces the policy in that gate (one place that allows, counts and limits), while A adds a second mechanism, a contextvar-scoped httpx GuardedTransport with its own host->destination map, that duplicates the gate. B also plans the T34 upgrade of old sessions (private -> all false, otherwise 'pre-notice' so the next session shows the notice) and corrects TASKS 3.2.1. A's per-destination agreement and B's four purposes are equivalent in effect; B's purpose names line up with T19's registry. One refinement from A is kept: the notice names 'your browser's speech service (Google in Chrome)' rather than asserting Google in every browser, and breaker fall-over may only move among allowed destinations.

verdicts.reasoning: Both chose the same design: cache only fixed sentences (nothing personal at rest, so erasure needs no voice step), server-side per-sentence assembly with recordings first and grouped remote TTS for unrecorded runs, WAV join with the stdlib and an X-Voiced header, Unicode-script detection for typed Tamil/Hindi, per-sentence language and origin, separate translated/reworded counters and truthful model/provider. A is more accurate on two points checked in code: the recordings are written by voice-worker/record_phrases.py at model.config.sampling_rate (Indic Parler-TTS), not the 24 kHz Gemini/Sarvam rate (gemini_tts.py RATE = 24000), so a one-time normalisation is required; B asserts both are already 24 kHz mono. And A keys the egress check on session_id, consistent with both teams' T25 (/speak requires session_id), while B adds a client-asserted SpeakIn.private flag, which the server cannot trust. A's tasks also map flags more finely. B contributes useful refinements: unvoiced sentences fall back to the browser voice (fully offline) rather than text only, detect_script lives in T01's shared vocab/language.py, done keeps 'language' for compatibility beside 'languages', the sentence record is the one stored in T11's Turn.reply, short scriptless replies keep the previous language, and an eval-replay test that every cache file written is in the fixed set. Final = A with those B refinements.

Per-sentence assembly lets free recordings win whenever they exist while keeping grouping's savings, and degrades to the browser voice. Per-sentence language and origin on the typed event (T28) fixes voice choice, captions, metrics and T25 attribution with one field; script detection is a few deterministic lines.

verdicts.reasoning: Both teams found the same faults (ad-hoc _event dicts and a hand-written AgentEvent union; streamTurn treats end-of-body as success; a VersionConflict at the final save becomes an 'error' after every sentence was spoken under HTTP 200; idempotency planned only on the route Talk never calls; board.notify reaches only current subscribers; Talk keeps only the latest queued utterance) and both chose a Pydantic discriminated union with a terminal Done/Error rule, client_turn_id with last_turn replay in the session document (0003), typed error codes, notice replay, an array queue and openapi-typescript generation. B fixes F-B1-008 at its root: it claims the turn with a version-guarded save before the first event, so a conflict is a real HTTP 409 before anything is spoken, and a different live turn gets 409 turn_in_progress (jobs.py confirms background jobs write only to the result board, not the session, so after the claim the only competing writers are other turns, which the claim excludes). A accepts the late conflict and softens it client-side (drop the unsaved reply, reload, speak a correction). B also honours Last-Event-ID on the notices EventSource, has a TurnWriter where T23's TurnClock plugs in, and extends response models to cohort and voice routes. A contributes what B leaves out: client-side conflict handling is still needed as a fallback (a stale-claim takeover or delete can still conflict at commit), honest 'expired' handling with a spoken message instead of a silent fresh start (B defers it to T18), and a finer task breakdown. Final = B's claim/commit design with A's client conflict fallback and expiry handling.

final.chosen: Typed TurnEvent union written by one TurnWriter, a terminal Done/Error rule, turn claim/commit keyed by client_turn_id with last_turn replay in the session document, typed error codes (409 before speaking, with a client fallback for late conflicts), notice replay on subscribe with Last-Event-ID, an array utterance queue, and OpenAPI-to-TypeScript generation checked in CI
final.why_chosen: Claiming the turn before speaking moves conflicts to a real 409 at request time, removing the 'spoken then discarded' case at its root; the recorded last turn gives idempotent retries on the route the Talk page uses, stored with the session so a replay can never disagree with the saved turn and works on every store. The terminal sentinel tells the client when to retry. One typed writer is where T23's TurnClock sits, and the same Pydantic models are exported to TypeScript, so Python and the browser cannot drift. No new runtime dependency.
